title: Most Enterprise Agentic Projects Are Doomed, Here's Why — Jess Grogan-Avignon & Jack Wang, Accenture

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on agent control planes in enterprises—progressive autonomy via shadow, advisory, and controlled-autonomy modes with kill switches and evidence-gated trust progression—which are harness architecture patterns. The entire discussion addresses internal enterprise workflows, governance, and operational challenges of deploying agentic AI at scale in large organizations. The talk spans rapid prototyping through the deployment-to-production gap and into ongoing operation with trust-building feedback loops. The content requires familiarity with enterprise IT governance and agent concepts but is strategic rather than implementation-deep. This is a conference presentation by two Accenture practitioners sharing enterprise deployment lessons. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Jess and Jack work with enormous enterprises where bad deployments can take down national infrastructure, so these organizations built layers of control, process, and governance—effective at human pace but increasingly a drag on AI value capture. Only 12% of companies are AI achievers while most are stuck piloting. They identify five enterprise tensions that predict agentic project success. Tension 1 (speed): approval infrastructure must become executable code, not sign-off chains; GitHub's 275 million weekly commits expose processes designed for human speed. Tension 2 (value): CFOs should think like VCs, backing a portfolio of AI bets rather than demanding committed returns; AI achievers show approximately 50% higher revenue growth from new capabilities. Tension 3 (delivery): agentic systems are non-deterministic with emergent behavior; teams need hypothesis-driven build-evaluate-iterate loops, not milestone programs. Tension 4 (trust): trust is built through progressive autonomy—an exposure ladder from shadow mode (agent runs alongside humans but cannot affect outcomes), to advisory mode (agent recommends, humans approve or reject), to controlled autonomy (agent triggers actions in narrow, low-risk scenarios with kill switches). Each step is gated by outcome evidence, not project plan completion. Tension 5 (moat): transactional memory—CRM, ERP, SOPs—is a floor, not a fortress; every competitor has one. The real moat is living memory: edge cases, corrections, emotional intent, and actual behavior at your specific scale, generated every time a customer touches your product. Every feature should either generate a feedback signal or deliver on what prior signals taught you. Their prescription: start now with hypothesis-driven delivery, make finance a transformation partner, make governance speed the CTO's top engineering problem, and recognize that the moat is what you learn and compound every day. The technology will keep accelerating; survivors will be those who learn to learn, build living memory through feedback loops, and cultivate trust. Bet like a VC, upgrade for machine speed, and engineer for trust with feedback from day one.

sections.title: Introduction: Enterprise Context and the Human-Pace Problem
sections.summary: Jess and Jack describe their world of enormous enterprises where bad deployments can take down national infrastructure. These organizations built layers of control and governance effective at human pace, but AI demands machine speed. Only 12% of companies are AI achievers; most are stuck piloting. The enterprise scaffold itself—governance, process, repeatability—is becoming the drag holding back AI value capture. They introduce five enterprise tensions that can predict project success before it starts.

sections.title: The 2-Week Build, 12-Month Production Story
sections.summary: They describe delivering an agentic solution integrated with a centralized AI gateway where every configuration change required manual review. The application took two weeks to build but twelve months to reach production because infrastructure, security, AI gateway, data governance, and application teams all needed to align. They compare this to Google search requiring three teams to review results, legal sign-off, and a two-week change freeze wait before displaying results.

sections.title: Tension 1: Approval Infrastructure as Executable Code
sections.summary: Handing AI coding agents to developers creates bottlenecks at code review and deployment. GitHub reported 1 billion commits in 2025 so far, averaging 275 million per week, on track for 14 billion by year end. Coding agents turn PMs, designers, and domain experts into builders, exploding deployable code supply. But approval and deployment infrastructure has not changed because processes were designed for human speed. The real tech debt is years of underinvestment in engineering automation and CI/CD. The pathway: every human process must become adaptable, executable code—not another meeting or sign-off chain.

sections.title: Tension 2: Finance Must Think Like a VC
sections.summary: Business cases raise right questions about ROI and oversight but assume scope, expected value, and cost are knowable upfront—backwards for AI where you learn by doing. When prototyping costs approach zero, entirely new product categories become economically viable. AI achievers show approximately 50% higher revenue growth from doing new things, not cost cutting. Emergent successes like Cursor, Claude Code, Walmart's trend scanner, and JP Morgan's productized tool show value was not planned on roadmaps. The CFO must think like a VC: back a portfolio, accept most bets will not pay off, and chase the ones that compound exponentially.

sections.title: Tension 3: Hypothesis-Driven Delivery
sections.summary: Data scientists and ML engineers already work with hypothesis, experiment, and statistical confidence—the right language for agentic delivery. Models are non-deterministic and agent behavior is emergent, so projects cannot be scoped as feature builds or milestoned as fixed programs. Most delivery energy is consumed bridging the gap between how systems work and stakeholder expectations. Teams need small build-evaluate-iterate loops generating fast evidence, with members comfortable with ambiguity who can articulate what they learned and translate statistical numbers into stakeholder confidence.

sections.title: Tension 4: Building Trust Through Progressive Autonomy
sections.summary: Society is collectively learning to trust AI—no one cross-checks Google results, and AI tool users rarely review every code output. Agentic delivery acts as deposits or withdrawals into a trust account with stakeholders, leadership, and end customers. Many companies still see agents as traditional automation you build and turn on, but agent behavior is emergent and cannot be fully foreseen or tested upfront. The solution is progressive autonomy via an exposure ladder: shadow mode (agent runs alongside human processes but cannot affect outcomes, generating iteration signals), advisory mode (agent recommends live, humans approve or reject, providing further signals), then controlled autonomy (agent triggers actions in narrow low-risk scenarios with kill switches). Each step is gated by evidence in outcomes—not project plan completion or pass-fail testing. Engineer for trust, not just for completion.

sections.title: Tension 5: The Real Moat Is Living Memory
sections.summary: In a recursive world where AI codes AI, anything shipped can be cloned the minute it goes viral. Existing enterprise knowledge—CRM, ERP, SOPs—is transactional memory that got you to the table, but every competitor has a version; it is a floor, not a fortress. The real moat is living memory: edge cases, corrections, emotional intent, and actual behavior at your specific scale and context, generated when customers touch your product. The day you ship is not the finish line—it is when the race begins. Every feature should either generate a feedback signal or deliver on what prior signals taught you. Feedback is not an option; feedback is the only moat.

sections.title: Prescription: Applying the Five Tensions
sections.summary: They summarize the five tensions—speed, value, delivery, trust, moat—and prescribe three actions. First, start now: deliver differently, measure in confidence, shape projects around hypotheses, and run small experimentation loops. Second, make finance a transformation partner: create a portfolio of AI bets across the organization rather than justifying each in isolation, and see value beyond cost out. Third, make governance speed the CTO's top engineering problem—the ultimate technical debt to rectify. For CEOs: the moat is not what you hold from yesterday but what you are learning and compounding every day. Survivors will be those who learn to learn, build living memory through feedback loops, and cultivate trust. The prescription: bet like a VC, upgrade for machine speed, and engineer for trust with the feedback loop from day one.
